name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q01 - Correct IUPAC name of branched alkane

questiontext.text: Which of the following is the correct IUPAC name?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the IUPAC rules of nomenclature for branched alkanes, when more than one type of substituent is attached to the parent carbon chain, the substituents must be listed in alphabetical order. Numerical prefixes such as di, tri, or tetra are ignored when determining the alphabetical sequence.

Step 2: Numbering of the Parent Chain
The parent chain consists of seven carbon atoms (heptane). Numbering from one end yields locants 3, 4, and 4 (giving the locant set 3, 4, 4), whereas numbering from the opposite end yields locants 4, 4, and 5 (giving the locant set 4, 4, 5). The set (3, 4, 4) is preferred by the lowest locant rule at the first point of difference.

Step 3: Alphabetical Ordering and Final Conclusion
Alphabetically, 'ethyl' precedes 'methyl'. Thus, the ethyl group is written before the dimethyl group in the complete systematic name. Combining the correct numbering and alphabetical order gives 3-Ethyl-4, 4-dimethylheptane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q02 - IUPAC name of oxo carboxylic acid

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of Principal Functional Group
The molecule contains both a carboxylic acid group (\(-\mathrm{COOH}\)) and a ketonic carbonyl group (\(>\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}\)). According to IUPAC priority rules, the carboxylic acid functional group has higher seniority than the keto group and serves as the principal functional group providing the suffix "-oic acid".

Step 2: Numbering the Carbon Chain
The principal functional group carbon is assigned locant 1. Numbering along the continuous 5-carbon chain gives: C1 at \(-\mathrm{COOH}\), C2 at \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\), C3 at \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\), C4 at \(-\mathrm{C}(=\mathrm{O})-\), and C5 at \(-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

Step 3: Naming the Substituent and Parent Chain
The ketonic oxygen at carbon-4 is treated as a substituent designated by the prefix "oxo". With a five-carbon saturated chain as the parent alkane (pentanoic acid), the correct systematic name is 4-oxopentanoic acid.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q03 - IUPAC name of trisubstituted benzene derivative

questiontext.text: The IUPAC name for

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Locant Assignment
The benzene ring contains three substituents: a chloro group, a nitro group, and a methyl group. Numbering begins at the carbon carrying the chloro substituent as C1 and proceeds clockwise towards the nitro group to give the lowest locant set (1, 2, 4). Other numbering directions produce higher locant sets such as (1, 3, 4) or (1, 4, 5).

Step 2: Alphabetical Ordering of Substituents
The substituents present are chloro at C1, nitro at C2, and methyl at C4. In the systematic IUPAC name, substituents are arranged alphabetically: "chloro" comes before "methyl", which in turn comes before "nitro".

Step 3: Assembly of the Systematic Name
Combining the locants with the alphabetical order of prefixes and appending the parent name benzene yields 1-Chloro-4-methyl-2-nitrobenzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q04 - Electronegativity of carbon based on hybridisation

questiontext.text: Electronegativity of carbon atoms depends upon their state of hybridisation. In which of the following compounds, the carbon marked with asterisk is most electronegative?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The electronegativity of a carbon atom increases with an increase in the fractional s-character of its hybrid orbitals. Electrons in an s orbital are held closer and more tightly to the nucleus than those in p orbitals. Consequently, electronegativity follows the sequence: \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) (25% s-character) < \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) (33.3% s-character) < \(\mathrm{sp}\) (50% s-character).

Step 2: Evaluation of Hybridisation States
In \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - *\text{CH}_2 - \text{CH}_3\), the asterisked carbon forms four single sigma bonds and is \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) hybridised.
In \(\text{CH}_3 - *\text{CH} = \text{CH} - \text{CH}_3\), the asterisked carbon participates in a double bond with three sigma bonds and is \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridised.
In \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{CH} = *\text{CH}_2\), the asterisked carbon is also involved in a double bond and is \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridised.
In \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{C} \equiv *\text{CH}\), the asterisked carbon participates in a triple bond with two sigma bonds and is \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybridised.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybridised carbon in \(\text{CH}_3 - \text{CH}_2 - \text{C} \equiv *\text{CH}\) possesses the highest percentage of s-character (50%) and is therefore the most electronegative.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q05 - Compound not exhibiting functional group isomerism

questiontext.text: In which of the following, functional group isomerism is not possible?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Functional group isomerism occurs when two or more compounds share the same molecular formula but have different functional groups belonging to different homologous classes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Classes of Compounds
Alcohols exhibit functional group isomerism with ethers (both having the general formula \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n+2}\mathrm{O}\)).
Aldehydes exhibit functional group isomerism with ketones, cyclic ethers, or unsaturated alcohols (having the general formula \(\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}\mathrm{O}\)).
Cyanides (\(\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{N}\)) exhibit functional group isomerism with isocyanides (\(\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{N}\equiv\mathrm{C}\)).
Alkyl halides (\(\mathrm{R}-\mathrm{X}\)) consist of an alkyl group covalently bonded to a halogen atom. Since halogens are monovalent terminal atoms without multiple bonding arrangements or polyvalent connectivity within the carbon skeleton, they cannot rearrange to form an entirely different functional class with the same molecular formula.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Functional group isomerism is not possible in alkyl halides.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q06 - Extraction method for steam volatile essential oils

questiontext.text: The fragrance of flowers is due to the presence of some steam volatile organic compounds called essential oils. These are generally insoluble in water at room temperature but are miscible with water vapour in vapour phase. A suitable method for the extraction of these oils from the flowers is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Steam distillation is applied to separate substances that are steam volatile and practically immiscible with water. In steam distillation, the mixture boils when the sum of the vapour pressure of water (\(p_1\)) and the organic compound (\(p_2\)) equals the atmospheric pressure (\(P = p_1 + p_2\)), allowing the organic component to distil at a temperature well below its normal boiling point without undergoing thermal decomposition.

Step 2: Evaluation of Essential Oils
Essential oils from flowers are steam-volatile substances that are insoluble in liquid water at room temperature but miscible with steam in the vapour state. This matches the exact operational conditions required for steam distillation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The most suitable method for the extraction of these oils from flowers is steam distillation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q07 - Technique for forensic ink pigment analysis

questiontext.text: During hearing of a court case, the judge suspected that some changes in the documents had been carried out. He asked the forensic department to check the ink used at two different places. According to you which technique can give the best results?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thin layer chromatography (TLC) is an adsorption chromatography technique that enables the rapid, sensitive separation and micro-analysis of minute quantities of mixtures, such as dyes and ink pigments, on a thin adsorbent layer coated on a glass, plastic, or aluminium plate.

Step 2: Practical Application in Forensic Document Examination
Ink samples from questioned documents can be sampled in microscopic quantities (tiny punched dots) and dissolved in a suitable solvent without destroying the document. TLC separates the individual dye components based on their differential adsorption and mobility (\(R_f\) values). Comparing the chromatographic spot profiles and \(R_f\) values reliably reveals whether identical or different inks were used.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thin layer chromatography provides the best results for testing and comparing the inks.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q08 - Governing principle involved in paper chromatography

questiontext.text: The principle involved in paper chromatography is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromatographic techniques are classified into adsorption chromatography and partition chromatography depending on the physical nature of the stationary and mobile phases and the mechanism of separation.

Step 2: Mechanism of Paper Chromatography
Paper chromatography is an example of partition chromatography. In paper chromatography, a specially prepared chromatography paper contains water molecules bound tightly within the cellulose network, which acts as the stationary liquid phase. A developing solvent mixture acts as the mobile liquid phase. As the mobile phase travels up the paper by capillary action, components of the mixture partition continuously and differentially between the stationary water phase and the mobile liquid phase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The fundamental principle governing paper chromatography is partition.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q09 - Decreasing order of carbocation intermediate stability

questiontext.text:
What is the correct order of decreasing stability of the following cations.

\[ \begin{array}{c} \mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{CH}_3 \\ \mathrm{I}. \end{array} \]

\[ \begin{array}{c} \mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{OCH}_3 \\ \mathrm{II}. \end{array} \]

\[ \begin{array}{c} \mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{CH}_2 - \mathrm{OCH}_3 \\ \mathrm{III}. \end{array} \]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of Cation II
In cation II, \(\mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{OCH}_3\), the unshared electron pair on the adjacent oxygen atom is directly conjugated with the vacant p orbital of the positively charged carbon. Resonance delocalisation yields the canonical form \(\mathrm{CH}_3 - \mathrm{CH} = \overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{O}}\mathrm{CH}_3\), where every atom (carbon and oxygen) satisfies an octet of valence electrons. Because resonance stabilisation with complete octets is the most powerful stabilising factor, cation II is the most stable.

Step 2: Comparison of Cation I and Cation III
In cation I, \(\mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{CH}_3\), the secondary carbocation is stabilised by six hyperconjugative \(\alpha\)-hydrogens and the \(+\mathrm{I}\) inductive effect of two methyl groups.
In cation III, \(\mathrm{CH}_3 - \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}} - \mathrm{CH}_2 - \mathrm{OCH}_3\), the oxygen atom is separated from the carbocationic center by a \(-\mathrm{CH}_2-\) group, preventing resonance donation. Consequently, the strongly electronegative oxygen exerts a powerful electron-withdrawing \(-I\) inductive effect, which destabilises the positive charge relative to cation I.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of decreasing stability is \(\mathrm{II} > \mathrm{I} > \mathrm{III}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q10 - Correct IUPAC name for branched hexane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Expansion of Ethyl Groups
Expanding the ethyl substituents (\(-\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5 = -\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3\)) gives the complete structural formula:
\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3)-\mathrm{CH}_3\).

Step 2: Selection of the Longest Continuous Carbon Chain
Tracing the longest continuous carbon chain reveals six carbon atoms: starting from an ethyl carbon, through the two CH carbons, and terminating at the other ethyl carbon:
\(\overset{1}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3-\overset{2}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2-\overset{3}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\overset{4}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}(\mathrm{CH}_3)-\overset{5}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2-\overset{6}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\).
The parent chain is therefore hexane.

Step 3: Locating Substituents and Final Name
Two methyl substituents are attached at positions 3 and 4 of the six-carbon parent chain. Numbering from either end yields identical locants (3, 4). Thus, the correct systematic IUPAC name is 3,4-dimethylhexane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q11 - Carbon with greatest positive inductive charge

questiontext.text: In which of the following compounds the carbon marked with asterisk is expected to have greatest positive charge?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electronegative atoms pull electron density away from adjacent carbon atoms via the \(-I\) (electron-withdrawing inductive) effect. The inductive effect diminishes rapidly with distance along the carbon chain, but a stronger \(-I\) substituent creates a larger partial positive charge (\(\delta+\)) on C1, which in turn induces a larger residual partial positive charge (\(\delta\delta+\)) on the adjacent asterisk-marked C2 carbon.

Step 2: Evaluation of Substituent Effects
In \({}^*\mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{Cl}\), chlorine has higher electronegativity (3.16 on the Pauling scale) than bromine (2.96), so \(\mathrm{Cl}\) exerts a stronger \(-I\) effect than \(\mathrm{Br}\). Consequently, the induced positive charge transmitted to the terminal methyl carbon is larger in the chloroalkane than in \({}^*\mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{Br}\).
In \({}^*\mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{Mg}^{+}\mathrm{Cl}^{-}\), magnesium is electropositive relative to carbon (exerting a \(+I\) effect / partial negative charge onto the adjacent carbon).
In \({}^*\mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{3}\), alkyl groups exert a mild electron-donating \(+I\) effect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The asterisked carbon in \({}^*\mathrm{CH}_{3}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{Cl}\) experiences the greatest positive charge.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q12 - Stability of substituted carboxylate anion species

questiontext.text: Ionic species are stabilised by the dispersal of charge. Which of the following carboxylate ion is the most stable?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The stability of an anion increases when its negative charge is dispersed across other atoms. For carboxylate ions (\(-\mathrm{COO}^-\)), electron-withdrawing groups (\(-I\) effect) withdraw electron density from the carboxylate center, facilitating charge dispersal and increasing stability.

Step 2: Comparison of Inductive Effects
In acetate ion (\(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{COO}^-\)), the methyl group has an electron-donating \(+I\) effect, which intensifies the negative charge and decreases stability.
Halogens exert an electron-withdrawing \(-I\) effect. Fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine, so a fluoro substituent exerts a stronger \(-I\) effect than a chloro substituent.
In the difluoroacetate ion, two highly electronegative fluorine atoms are attached to the \(\alpha\)-carbon. The combined \(-I\) effect of two fluorine atoms is significantly greater than that of a single fluorine or chlorine atom, causing the greatest dispersal of negative charge.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The difluoroacetate ion, \(\begin{array}{c}\mathrm{F}\\\mathrm{F}\end{array}\mathrm{CH}-\overset{\mathrm{O}}{\underset{\mathrm{\parallel}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{O}^-\), is the most stable carboxylate ion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q13 - Intermediate formed in propene electrophilic addition

questiontext.text:
Electrophilic addition reactions proceed in two steps. The first step involves the addition of an electrophile. Name the type of intermediate formed in the first step of the following addition reaction.

\[ \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{HC}=\mathrm{CH}_2 + \mathrm{H}^+ \longrightarrow {?} \]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Mechanism of Electrophilic Attack
In the first step of an electrophilic addition to propene, the electrophile (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) attacks the electron-rich \(\pi\) bond. The \(\pi\) electrons can form a new \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}\) bond at either the terminal carbon (\(\mathrm{C}1\)) or the internal carbon (\(\mathrm{C}2\)).

Step 2: Stability of Possible Carbocation Intermediates
Addition of \(\mathrm{H}^+\) to the terminal carbon (\(\mathrm{C}1\)) generates a secondary carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), which has six \(\alpha\)-hydrogens for hyperconjugative delocalisation.
Conversely, addition of \(\mathrm{H}^+\) to the secondary carbon (\(\mathrm{C}2\)) would generate a primary carbocation, \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2\), which has only two \(\alpha\)-hydrogens and is significantly less stable.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because reaction pathways preferentially proceed via the more stable intermediate according to Markovnikov's rule, a 2° carbocation is formed in the first step.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q14 - Heterolytic fission representation of bromomethane bond

questiontext.text: Covalent bond can undergo fission in two different ways. The correct representation involving a heterolytic fission of \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{—Br}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Heterolytic Fission
In heterolytic bond fission, the covalent bond breaks unsymmetrically such that the shared pair of electrons is retained entirely by one of the bonded atoms, creating a cation and an anion. Curved arrows are used in reaction mechanisms to depict the flow of electron pairs, originating from the covalent bond and pointing toward the atom receiving the pair.

Step 2: Electronegativity and Electron Flow
Bromine is significantly more electronegative than carbon. During heterolysis of the \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Br}\) bond, the shared pair of electrons shifts to the bromine atom. This movement is shown by a curved arrow that starts at the \(\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{Br}\) bond and points directly to the bromine atom, yielding a methyl carbocation (\(\overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3\)) and a bromide anion (\(\mathrm{Br}^{\ominus}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct representation is \(\mathrm{CH}_3\overset{\curvearrowright}{-}\mathrm{Br} \longrightarrow \overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_3 + \mathrm{Br}^{\ominus}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q15 - Curved arrow representation in alkene electrophilic attack

questiontext.text: The addition of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to an alkene proceeds in two steps. The first step is the attack of \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion to \({>}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}{<}\) portion which can be shown as

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Curved Arrow Notation
In organic reaction mechanisms, curved arrows track the movement of electron pairs. An arrow must always originate from an electron-rich site (a nucleophilic source, such as a \(\pi\) electron cloud or a lone pair) and terminate at an electron-deficient site (an electrophile, such as a positively charged proton \(\mathrm{H}^+\)).

Step 2: Application to Alkene Protonation
In the first step of electrophilic addition, the \({>}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}{<}\) double bond acts as the nucleophile due to its loosely held \(\pi\) electrons. The proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) acts as the electrophile with an empty 1s orbital. Therefore, the curved arrow must originate from the \({>}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}{<}\) double bond and point towards the \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion. Drawing an arrow starting from \(\mathrm{H}^+\) is mechanistically incorrect because \(\mathrm{H}^+\) possesses no valence electrons to donate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct representation shows the curved arrow originating from the double bond towards the proton: \({>}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{C}{<} \xrightarrow{\curvearrowright} \mathrm{H}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q16 - Compounds containing carbons in same hybridisation

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds contain all the carbon atoms in the same hybridisation state?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The hybridisation state of a carbon atom is determined by the number of sigma (\(\sigma\)) bonds it forms: four \(\sigma\) bonds correspond to \(\mathrm{sp}^3\), three \(\sigma\) bonds correspond to \(\mathrm{sp}^2\), and two \(\sigma\) bonds correspond to \(\mathrm{sp}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Compound
In \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}\), every carbon atom forms two \(\sigma\) bonds and two \(\pi\) bonds. Thus, all four carbon atoms are in the \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybridisation state.
In \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_3\), the two methyl carbons form four \(\sigma\) bonds (\(\mathrm{sp}^3\)), whereas the two acetylenic carbons form two \(\sigma\) bonds (\(\mathrm{sp}\)). Hence, they have different hybridisation states.
In \(\mathrm{CH}_2 = \mathrm{C} = \mathrm{CH}_2\), the two terminal carbons are \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridised (forming three \(\sigma\) bonds), while the central carbon is \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybridised (forming two \(\sigma\) bonds). Hence, they are not all in the same state.
In \(\mathrm{CH}_2 = \mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH} = \mathrm{CH}_2\), each carbon atom forms three \(\sigma\) bonds and one \(\pi\) bond. Therefore, all four carbon atoms are in the \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridisation state.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C} \equiv \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{H}\) (all carbons \(\mathrm{sp}\)) and \(\mathrm{CH}_2 = \mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH} = \mathrm{CH}_2\) (all carbons \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)) have all their carbon atoms in the same hybridisation state.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q17 - Different spatial arrangement in wedge dash projections

questiontext.text: In which of the following representations given below spatial arrangement of group/ atom different from that given in structure 'A'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In three-dimensional tetrahedral wedge-dash representations of a chiral center, exchanging the positions of any two groups (a single interchange) inverts the configuration to its enantiomer (yielding a different spatial arrangement). Performing an even number of interchanges (such as two pairwise swaps) restores the original configuration (yielding the identical spatial arrangement).

Step 2: Configuration of Structure 'A'
Structure 'A' has a methyl group at the top in-plane, a hydrogen atom at the bottom-right in-plane, a bromine atom on the projecting wedge, and a chlorine atom on the receding dash.

Step 3: Comparative Analysis of Representations
Representation with methyl at the top, bromine at the right, hydrogen on the wedge, and chlorine on the dash: Here, hydrogen and bromine are swapped (1 interchange). A single interchange produces the opposite enantiomer, which represents a different spatial arrangement.
Representation with methyl at the top, bromine at the right, chlorine on the wedge, and hydrogen on the dash: Starting from structure 'A', swapping hydrogen and bromine (1st interchange) and then swapping hydrogen and chlorine (2nd interchange) results in this representation. Two interchanges preserve the original configuration, so its spatial arrangement is identical to structure 'A'.
Representation with methyl at the top, hydrogen at the right, chlorine on the wedge, and bromine on the dash: Here, chlorine and bromine are swapped (1 interchange), producing the opposite enantiomer with a different spatial arrangement.
Representation with bromine at the top, hydrogen at the right, methyl on the wedge, and chlorine on the dash: Here, bromine and methyl are swapped (1 interchange), which inverts the configuration and gives a different spatial arrangement.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The representations with a single interchange have a spatial arrangement different from that of structure 'A'.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_MCQ_Q18 - Species groups containing only electrophilic reagents

questiontext.text: Electrophiles are electron seeking species. Which of the following groups contain only electrophiles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrophiles are electron-deficient chemical species that seek electron pairs. They include positively charged ions with vacant valence orbitals and neutral molecules possessing an incomplete octet or an electron-deficient central atom (Lewis acids). Conversely, species with lone pairs of electrons or negative charges capable of donating electrons act as nucleophiles (Lewis bases).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Group
In \(\mathrm{BF}_3, \mathrm{NH}_3, \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\): While \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) is an electrophile (incomplete octet on boron), both ammonia (\(:\mathrm{NH}_3\)) and water (\(\mathrm{H}_2\ddot{\mathrm{O}}:\)) possess unshared electron pairs on nitrogen and oxygen and act as nucleophiles. Thus, this group does not contain exclusively electrophiles.
In \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3, \mathrm{SO}_3, \mathrm{NO}_2^+\): \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3\) is an electron-deficient molecule with six valence electrons around aluminium (Lewis acid); \(\mathrm{SO}_3\) has a highly electrophilic central sulfur atom bonded to three strongly electronegative oxygen atoms; \(\mathrm{NO}_2^+\) is the nitronium cation carrying a positive charge. All three species are electrophiles.
In \(\mathrm{NO}_2^+, \mathrm{CH}_3^+, \mathrm{CH}_3 - \overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}} = \mathrm{O}\): All three are carbocations or positively charged acylium/nitronium ions possessing an electron deficiency. All three species are electrophiles.
In \(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5^-, \dot{\mathrm{C}}_2\mathrm{H}_5, \mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5^+\): The ethyl carbanion (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5^-\)) carries a negative charge and an unshared pair of electrons, making it a nucleophile. Thus, this group does not contain exclusively electrophiles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The groups containing exclusively electrophilic species are \(\mathrm{AlCl}_3, \mathrm{SO}_3, \mathrm{NO}_2^+\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_2^+, \mathrm{CH}_3^+, \mathrm{CH}_3 - \overset{\oplus}{\mathrm{C}} = \mathrm{O}\).
